coping_reactions.description: Day-to-day, planless attitude and collective thinking
coping_reactions.supporting_quote: his coping reactions will be a provisional attitude towards life as basic reaction, together with a 'planless, day-to-day attitude toward life' and 'collective thinking'
coping_reactions.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, consciousness and self-regulation (pp. 27-42). Nova Science Publishers.

coping_reactions.supporting_quote: idealisation and fanaticism as main forms of activism
coping_reactions.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, consciousness and self-regulation (pp. 27-42). Nova Science Publishers.
Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, consciousness and self-regulation (pp. 27-42). Nova Science Publishers.

coping_reactions.description: Loss of interest and belief in meaning
coping_reactions.supporting_quote: Fatalism, loss of interest, apathy and probably nihilism can be seen as forms of freezing reactions.
coping_reactions.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, consciousness and self-regulation (pp. 27-42). Nova Science Publishers.

meaning_definitions.definition: Most valuable, realistic possibility in given situation for which one should decide
meaning_definitions.supporting_quote: We define meaning as 'the most valuable, realistic possibility of the given situation, for which I feel I should decide myself'. Existential meaning is therefore what is possible here and now, on the basis of facts and reality.
meaning_definitions.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, consciousness and self-regulation (pp. 27-42). Nova Science Publishers.

meaning_definitions.definition: Overall meaning from creator, perceived through faith
meaning_definitions.supporting_quote: Besides this existential meaning there is an ontological meaning. This is the overall meaning in which I find myself and which does not depend on me. It is the philosophical and religious meaning, the meaning the creator of the world must have had in mind.
meaning_definitions.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, consciousness and self-regulation (pp. 27-42). Nova Science Publishers.

meaning_definitions.definition: A possibility against the background of reality
meaning_definitions.supporting_quote: Viktor Frankl once defined meaning as 'a possibility against the background of reality'.
meaning_definitions.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The existential fundamental motivations structuring the motivational process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, consciousness and self-regulation (pp. 27-42). Nova Science Publishers.

related_themes.description: Finiteness creates imperative to utilize life meaningfully
related_themes.supporting_quote: The real impulse, however, and the dynamics of the search for meaning might stem from the transitoriness of human life. Life exists in time and is as such always unique. This is exactly what gives it the quality of urgency
related_themes.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What are we looking for when we search for meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306-314.

related_themes.description: Realized opportunities saved into reality transcend transitoriness
related_themes.supporting_quote: The realised opportunity, however, which has been saved into reality, has been lifted out of transitoriness, because it has been irreversibly done. For 'having been is also a kind of being – perhaps the surest kind'
related_themes.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What are we looking for when we search for meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306-314.

related_themes.theme: Conscience and sensitivity as organs of meaning
related_themes.description: Internal capacity for reducing complexity to livable proportions
related_themes.supporting_quote: To define and redefine this continually is an extremely complex task for which we possess an inner organ of perception capable of reducing this complexity to livable proportions: our sensitivity as well as our moral conscience.
related_themes.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The existential fundamental motivations structuring the motivational process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, consciousness and self-regulation (pp. 27-42). Nova Science Publishers.

related_themes.description: Illustration of ontological vs existential meaning in work
related_themes.supporting_quote: It was at the time when the cathedral at Chartres was being built... The man looked up at him, wiped the sweat from his brow and said: 'I am working at a cathedral.'
related_themes.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The existential fundamental motivations structuring the motivational process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, consciousness and self-regulation (pp. 27-42). Nova Science Publishers.

four_fundamental_realities.description: Four cornerstones of existence according to modern existential analytical theory
four_fundamental_realities.source_quote: All preconditions of existence can be summarized in four fundamental structures, the 'cornerstones of existence': • the world in its factuality and potentiality • life with its network of relationships and its feelings • being oneself as a unique, autonomous person • the wider context in which to place oneself = development through one's activities, opening one's future
four_fundamental_realities.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 31.

continuous_confrontation.description: Existence requires continuous confrontation and dialogical exchange with these dimensions
continuous_confrontation.source_quote: Existence in our understanding requires a continuous confrontation and a dialogical exchange with each of these four dimensions. It is on this basis that the subject forms his or her specific notions about reality.
continuous_confrontation.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 31.

dual_nature.description: These realities are both challenging and structures to entrust oneself to
dual_nature.source_quote: These four realities challenge the person to respond, they ask for his or her inner consent, activate his or her inner freedom. But they are not only challenging dimensions – they are also structures which, at the same time, allow one to entrust oneself to each of these given realities.
dual_nature.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 31.

realities.reality: World in its factuality and potentiality
Life with its network of relationships and feelings
Being oneself as unique, autonomous person
Wider context = development through activities, opening future

meaning_structure.description: Four aspects inherent in psychological understanding of meaning

aspects.supporting_quote: Firstly it is objective 'on the basis of its situational reference'
aspects.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What are we looking for when we search for meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306-314.

aspects.description: Related to person and linkages of situation
aspects.supporting_quote: Secondly, meaning is relative, with regard to the person it is relating to, as well as to further linkages of the situation itself.
aspects.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What are we looking for when we search for meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306-314.

aspects.description: Can only be recognized by person in the situation
aspects.supporting_quote: Thirdly, it is subjective, in that it can only be recognised and realised by the person involved in the respective situation.
aspects.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What are we looking for when we search for meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306-314.

aspects.supporting_quote: meaning is, fourthly, always appellative by its character of challenge, urging the subject with its typical call to 'do something with me!'
aspects.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What are we looking for when we search for meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306-314.

phenomenological_understanding.description: Meaning must be found not invented, through personal evidence
phenomenological_understanding.supporting_quote: Experience shows that meaning can only be accepted when it has passed the 'needle's eye of personal evidence', whereby alone the relevance of a new meaning becomes intelligible.
phenomenological_understanding.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What are we looking for when we search for meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306-314.

threefold_question_structure.description: Three phenomena preceding question of meaning

phenomena.description: Network of effects between person and world
phenomena.supporting_quote: Three phenomena precede the question of meaning, enclosing the essence of the question like a three-sided pyramid. These are the three experiences man is always exposed to: 1) He observes effects.
phenomena.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What are we looking for when we search for meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306-314.

phenomena.description: Things and events have different worth
phenomena.supporting_quote: 2) He experiences different grades of value for things and events.
phenomena.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What are we looking for when we search for meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306-314.

phenomena.description: Present/future effects and right to live
phenomena.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What are we looking for when we search for meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306-314.

personal_existential_analysis_process.description: Three-step method for engaging personal potential

steps.name: Recognizing
steps.description: Perceiving worth, value, or challenge that speaks to us
steps.supporting_quote: Recognizing something in its worth or value, in as far as it speaks to us. This is often a challenge demanding action on our part.
steps.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The art of involving the person: Fundamental existential motivations as the structure of the motivational process. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), 25-36.

steps.name: Harmonizing
steps.description: Bringing perceived value into accordance with inner reality
steps.supporting_quote: Harmonizing. Bringing the perceived value, challenge or meaning into accordance with one's inner reality, i.e., examining the consistency with the rest of our values, with attitudes, abilities and capabilities and with our conscience.
steps.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The art of involving the person: Fundamental existential motivations as the structure of the motivational process. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), 25-36.

steps.name: Giving inner consent
steps.description: Presence of inner person in actions through consent
steps.supporting_quote: The final step in the development of motivation is the inner consent to one's own active involvement. This consent and the act of harmonizing the new value with inner (already existing personal) reality leads to the presence of the inner person in one's actions.
steps.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The art of involving the person: Fundamental existential motivations as the structure of the motivational process. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), 25-36.

structure_of_will.description: Four elements constituting free and realistic will

elements.description: Real ability and capacity of the subject
elements.supporting_quote: Free and realistic will is based on three more elements: 1. on the real ability and capacity of the subject;
elements.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The art of involving the person: Fundamental existential motivations as the structure of the motivational process. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), 25-36.

elements.description: Perception of situational value through feeling
elements.supporting_quote: 2. on the emotional perception of the situational value;
elements.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The art of involving the person: Fundamental existential motivations as the structure of the motivational process. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), 25-36.

elements.description: Agreement with concepts of life and morality
elements.supporting_quote: 3. on the inner permission for that act, emerging from an agreement with one's concepts of life and morality.
elements.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The art of involving the person: Fundamental existential motivations as the structure of the motivational process. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), 25-36.

elements.supporting_quote: Frankl saw meaning as the motor in free will.
elements.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The art of involving the person: Fundamental existential motivations as the structure of the motivational process. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), 25-36.

loss_of_meaning_categories.description: Three categories where meaning is explicitly lost

categories.description: During illness, suffering, death or sorrow
categories.supporting_quote: In this description of loss of meaning three categories: 1) loss of value, 2) loss of orientation and 3) loss of relations are contained
categories.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What are we looking for when we search for meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306-314.

categories.description: Vacuum when work loses quality of necessity
categories.supporting_quote: Loss of meaning, however, is also a frequent phenomenon in the area of work. Not even success serves as protection. Just at the point where work loses its quality of necessity for life, a vacuum of orientation is formed
categories.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What are we looking for when we search for meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306-314.

categories.description: Living without relating in consumption culture
categories.supporting_quote: Besides loss of value and lack of orientation in work, lack of relations is another phenomenon causing the existential vacuum. This abounds wherever life is experienced. Living without relating dwindles to boring and joyless consumption.
categories.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What are we looking for when we search for meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306-314.

loss_of_meaning_categories.description: Loss of meaning during illness, suffering, death, or sorrow
loss_of_meaning_categories.source_quote: We observe that the question explicitly forces itself upon man during phases when meaning is lost (Frankl, 1982a, pp. 18ff.; Längle, 1985, p. 85). Here primarily losses of value should be mentioned: During illness, suffering, death or sorrow, which call for a special attitude in man.
loss_of_meaning_categories.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 308.

loss_of_meaning_categories.description: Lack of orientation in work, having everything to live from but nothing to live for
loss_of_meaning_categories.source_quote: Loss of meaning, however, is also a frequent phenomenon in the area of work. Not even success serves as protection. Just at the point where work loses its quality of necessity for life, a vacuum of orientation is formed and causes the afflicted person to indeed have everything he can live from, but nothing more he can live for (Frankl, 1982b, p. 11; pp. 239ff.).
loss_of_meaning_categories.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 308.

loss_of_meaning_categories.description: Living without relating, leading to emptiness and lack of meaning
loss_of_meaning_categories.source_quote: Besides loss of value and lack of orientation in work, lack of relations is another phenomenon causing the existential vacuum (Frankl, 1982a, pp. 7, 18f.). This abounds wherever life is experienced. Living without relating dwindles to boring and joyless consumption.
loss_of_meaning_categories.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 308.

meaning_characteristics.description: Meaning is based on situational reference
meaning_characteristics.source_quote: Accordingly, the psychological understanding of meaning always has four aspects: Firstly it is objective 'on the basis of its situational reference' (Frankl, 1982a, p. 56).
meaning_characteristics.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 308.

meaning_characteristics.description: Meaning is relative to the person and situation linkages
meaning_characteristics.source_quote: Secondly, meaning is relative, with regard to the person it is relating to, as well as to further linkages of the situation itself.
meaning_characteristics.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 308.

meaning_characteristics.description: Meaning can only be recognized and realized by the person involved
meaning_characteristics.source_quote: Thirdly, it is subjective, in that it can only be recognised and realised by the person involved in the respective situation.
meaning_characteristics.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 308.

meaning_characteristics.description: Meaning has a challenging character that urges action
meaning_characteristics.source_quote: meaning is, fourthly, always appellative by its character of challenge (Frankl, 1982a, pp. 52-57), urging the subject with its typical call to 'do something with me!'
meaning_characteristics.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 308.

applications_beyond_therapy.description: Fundamental existential motivations apply to all person-centered relations
applications_beyond_therapy.source_quote: As existential basics they are important in all relations where the person stands in the center: education, pastoral counselling, management trainings, prevention of diseases, coaching, organisational structures etc.

coding_guidelines.application: Use this codebook to identify and code participant testimony related to the four fundamental motivations
coding_guidelines.hierarchical_structure: Code using FM1-FM4 as primary domains, with sub-codes for needs, outcomes, actions, and coping reactions

coding_guidelines.phenomenological_coding: Attend to phenomenological understanding of meaning - not as subjective attribution but as discovered through personal evidence and trans-subjective reality
coding_guidelines.exclusion_criteria: Only code content that directly relates to the described themes with supporting evidence from source materials

version_notes.v3.0: Initial codebook based on Längle (2011). Includes all four fundamental motivations with existential questions, needs, positive/negative outcomes, active participation elements, motivational process steps, and structure of will.
version_notes.v3.1: Integrated Längle (2003). Added: expanded theoretical foundation with being-in-the-world, interpersonal paradigm, provocation concept; refined motivational process descriptions; expanded FM2 with carpe diem and life reverberation; added histrionic disorders and suicidal tendencies to negative outcomes; expanded FM4 with self-transcendence emphasis and organ of perception for meaning; enhanced all four FMs with additional source quotes and refined descriptions.
version_notes.v3.2: Integrated Längle (2002). MAJOR ADDITIONS: Definition of Existential Analysis; phenomenological approach explanation (nous, epoché); inner consent framework with double dialogue; comprehensive coping reactions framework for ALL four FMs (basic reaction, activism, aggression, freezing, insufficient coping outcomes); existential claim concept; motivation components; applications beyond therapy; refined active participation terminology (tolerate, delimitate, correspondence); enhanced pathic dimension descriptions.
version_notes.v3.3: Integrated Längle (1992). MAJOR ADDITIONS: Comprehensive meaning framework including four aspects of meaning (objective, relative, subjective, appellative); phenomenological understanding of meaning as discovered rather than invented; personal evidence concept; threefold question of meaning (ontological, axiological, existential/ethical) with direct correspondence to FM1-FM4; three experiences preceding meaning (effects, value, consequences); loss of meaning categories (loss of value, loss of orientation, loss of relations) linked to Frankl's value categories; steps to finding meaning in psychotherapy; will to be, will to value, will to the right integrated into motivational theory; dynamics of search for meaning including transitoriness and urgency; death and transcendence understanding; enhanced each FM with corresponding level of meaning question; added meaning as orientation, meaning as value, meaning as relations descriptions.
version_notes.v4.0-MERGED: Comprehensive merger of three parallel codebook development paths (v1.3, v2.0, v3.3). Integrates: (1) v1.3's conceptual clarity and version tracking, (2) v2.0's systematic coding structure and practical application guidelines, (3) v3.3's comprehensive theoretical foundation and phenomenological depth. Result: A unified codebook suitable for rigorous academic research and practical therapeutic application.

notes: Version 1.3 is a metadata update documenting both the 2002 and 2011 versions of the same source.
Längle (2002) was a conference paper presented in Moscow (June 2002). Längle (2011) is the published book chapter with identical content.
No new substantive content was added in Version 1.3 - this update maintains transparency in citation tracking.
Version 1.2 added crucial detail about the motivational process and dialogical structure of existence.
Major additions in 1.2: Three-step motivational process (recognizing, harmonizing, inner consent); Four-element structure of will; Interpersonal paradigm; Assessment questions for each FM.
The codebook includes clear operational questions for assessing each FM in participant testimony.
The shift from Frankl's individualistic 'will to meaning' to modern EA's interpersonal/dialogical paradigm is documented.
The concept of 'provocation' as starting point for motivation provides a key indicator for coding participant responses.
Future versions will continue to add depth as more sources are incorporated, particularly focusing on clinical applications and specific indicators.
Version 4.0-MERGED represents the integration of three parallel codebook developments, each with unique strengths.
